lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Application or project: noticing hazards early

standardsRefs: Ready for Life v1, Grade 4 Unit 1: Home Care Routines That Last
objective: Learners walk through one real shared space with a trusted adult's permission, identify at least three specific hazards, such as trip hazards, blocked exits, or unsecured items, using a simple urgency rating, and report each finding to a trusted adult without touching, moving, or attempting to fix any hazard themselves.
scenario: A trusted adult agrees to a hazard walk-through of one shared space in the household, such as a hallway, stairwell, or main living area. The learner looks closely for anything that could cause a fall, burn, cut, or other injury, rates how urgent each hazard is, and reports the full list to the adult instead of handling any hazard directly.
safetyNotes: A trusted adult walks through the space together with the learner for the entire hazard walk-through.
The learner points out or describes each hazard but never touches, moves, plugs in, unplugs, or attempts to fix anything themselves.
If a hazard involves electricity, water near an outlet, or a blocked exit, the learner steps back and lets the adult handle it immediately rather than finishing the rest of the walk-through first.

simulationAlternative.description: If a real walk-through isn't possible right now, the learner instead studies a printed or hand-drawn floor plan of a household space, real or one they know well, and marks three specific spots where a hazard like a trip risk, a blocked exit, or an unsecured item could realistically occur, explaining the urgency rating they would give each one.

materials: one real shared space to walk through
paper or a notes app for recording hazards and urgency ratings

tasks.directions: Before walking through the space, think about what kinds of hazards you already know to look for.

prompts.text: List three types of hazards you already know how to spot, such as something you could trip on, something hot, or something blocking a door.

tasks.directions: With your adult, walk through the shared space slowly and point out anything that could cause a fall, burn, cut, or other injury, without touching it.

prompts.text: I pointed out or described each hazard out loud instead of touching, moving, or fixing it myself.
I found at least three specific hazards, not vague ones like 'it's messy.'
My adult confirmed or corrected each hazard I pointed out before we moved to the next one.

tasks.directions: For each hazard you found, rate how urgent it is using a simple scale and note where exactly it is located.

prompts.text: List each hazard you found with its exact location and an urgency rating of low, medium, or high, based on how likely it is to cause an injury soon.
Pick the single highest-urgency hazard on your list and explain the specific reason it earned that rating instead of a lower one.

tasks.directions: Think about the difference between noticing a hazard early and only noticing it after something goes wrong.

prompts.text: Explain why rating a hazard's urgency and reporting it right away matters more than waiting until the hazard causes an actual injury, using the highest-urgency hazard you found as your example.

remediation: If a learner's hazard list is vague, such as 'messy area' or 'stuff around,' instead of specific and actionable, reteach with a two-question filter for each spot: could this specific thing make someone fall, get burned, or get cut, and exactly where is it, walking through one already-identified hazard together before the learner continues the rest of the space alone with the adult present.
extension: Have the learner repeat the hazard walk-through in a second shared space and compare the two spaces' highest-urgency hazard, explaining which space needs attention sooner and why.
